title: Acts, looking back
hook: wind, fire, a road, a shipwreck, and a door left open in Rome
tomorrow: six practices. which one actually stayed?

segments.voice: Yesterday, five objects and one week: a donkey, a towel, a garden, a cross, a garden again. The week that turned the world. Today, how it left the garden.
screen: `THE WEEK THAT TURNED THE WORLD.` → `HOW IT LEFT THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Some things only reach you by hand: a recipe card in a grandmother's writing, a song a friend once played you in the car, a joke that's been through six group chats. Acts is the story of how a story from one garden in Jerusalem traveled. Wind, fire, a road, a shipwreck, and a door left open in Rome.
screen: `SOME THINGS COME BY HAND.` → `WIND, FIRE, A ROAD.` → `A SHIPWRECK, A DOOR.`

segments.voice: Before he's taken up, Jesus gives a map: “ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.” Acts follows it outward: wind and fire at Pentecost; Saul thrown down on the Damascus road, who becomes Paul and carries the story across the sea; a shipwreck where everyone reaches land; and Rome. The question underneath: who is the story for? Paul answers in Athens, speaking to people who didn't share his scriptures. God, he says, “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth.” One blood. One human family. Then he does something worth telling a friend: he quotes their own poets back to them, “as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.” Now a neighbor. In the Buddhist scriptures, the Buddha sends out his first monks with words that sound close: go and wander “for the gain of the many, for the welfare of the many, out of compassion for the world.” Shared ground: a teaching not kept in one room, carried on foot, for the good of everyone. An honest difference: the monks carry a path to walk, the Dhamma; the witnesses in Acts carry news of a person, Jesus, risen. And Acts doesn't really end. Paul is in Rome under guard, preaching “with all confidence, no man forbidding him,” and the book stops. The door stays open, hand to hand, to whoever is listening now.
screen: `TO THE UTTERMOST PART.` · `OF ONE BLOOD, ALL NATIONS.` · `A NEIGHBOR: FOR THE WELFARE OF THE MANY.` · `NO MAN FORBIDDING HIM.` · then, large: `THE STORY REACHED HERE.`

segments.voice: Trace how this story reached you, if it did: a person, a place, a book, a song. Follow the line back as far as it goes and name each hand it passed through. If one of them is only a text away, send them one line of thanks; if you pray, thank God for them by name.
Acts. The book that follows the first witnesses outward from Jerusalem, and ends with Paul in Rome and the door still open.
Your line: the story reached here. One blood, every nation, hand to hand. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: a classmate from a Buddhist family says, "my grandma says the Buddha sent his monks out for the welfare of the many. sounds like your Acts." what's a fair reply?
options: they're the same message, just in different words.
yes, both send people out for the good of many; the monks carry a path, Acts carries news of a person.
no, the two have nothing in common at all.
fork.reveal: both send their message out on foot, for everyone. the honest difference: the Buddha's monks carry the Dhamma, a path; the witnesses in Acts carry news of Jesus, risen.

chat.says: nia asked how i even got into all this faith stuff. i said "pop?" and then totally blanked.
options: Trace it back for her: Pop, the choir, whoever handed it on. Acts is exactly that, hand to hand.
Say it's just how you were raised. Faith isn't really something people pass along.
Lead with the best argument for God. Stories about people don't really count.
chat.meaning: Acts follows the story hand to hand, city to city, and Paul speaks to Athenians in their own poets' words. Naming who passed it on is honest.

Samaria.meaning: the region just north of Judaea

Pentecost.meaning: the feast when the Spirit came on Jesus's followers

Athens.meaning: the Greek city where Paul spoke about one human family

Dhamma.meaning: the Buddha's teaching, the path his followers walk
